newsitem.title: JAPAN: MIM news seen positive for LME zinc prices.
newsitem.headline: MIM news seen positive for LME zinc prices.

text.p: News that Australian miner MIM Holdings Ltd told European smelters it would cut supplies of zinc concentrates by half this year was positive for the market, Japanese traders said on Monday.

There was no consensus, however, that the comments from the annual America Zinc Association conference in Arizona would contribute directly to further gains in London Metal Exchange LME) zinc prices after Friday's rally, especially since MIM had already announced in December that it would cut zinc ore output at its Hilton mine.
Another trader said, however, that the news was simply an extension of the output cut announcement in December and was thus already factored into the market.

Traders in Japan nevertheless agreed that zinc prices appeared set for further gains in the days ahead, after LME benchmark three-month zinc rallied strongly on Friday to a fresh two-year high of $1,174 a tonne.
It retraced slightly by the end of the afternoon London kerb to close at $1,169, up $33.
On Monday, in thinly traded Tokyo hours, zinc was quoted at $1,170/75 at 0700 GMT.
MIM expects production of 360,000 tonnes of zinc concentrates in the year up to June, 1997 down from 410,000 tonnes the year before.

On Monday, MIM chief executive Nick Stump told Reuters the company was also shifting to the Asian market, as there was a clear advantage in terms of freight costs in shipping more concentrates to Asia at the expense of Europe.

"I think it'll probably be a favourable factor," said one source at a large Japanese trade house of today's news about MIM's European shipments, although he added it was unclear what immediate impact it would have on the market.
Traders said LME zinc was poised to test its January 1995 highs at $1,230 to $1,240, although one trader expected interim resistance at $1,190 and $1,220.

Traders around Asia said the willingness of Chinese zinc producers to take advantage of current high international prices was encouraging a flow of the metal out of China, much of it going to regional end users, but some also to Singapore warehouses.
One buyer said he was paying Chinese trading houses LME cash prices less $18 to $20 a tonne for the Chinese product.

Chinese producers were "very happy to sell at these prices," he said, though he added it was easier to keep the Chinese zinc he has been buying off-warrant and sell directly to his customers. He expected LME zinc stocks to rise by around 3,000 tonnes, on Tuesday.

Vinod Kumar, director of Donald McCarthy in Singapore said he expected LME copper stocks to rise by between 10,000 to 12,000 tonnes. This follows a sharp increase of 26,100 tonnes, to a total of 191,750 tonnes on Friday.
Kumar said Singapore warehouses have healthy stocks of 45,000 tonnes of coper, most controlled by one trading house now asking a premium of $50 a tonne above the LME cash price.
"On a day-to-day basis, the backwardation in Singapore is $23, so the tightness is there and should remain," Kumar said.

The LME copper backwardation eased last week from a high of $345 to dip briefly below $195, before strengthening once again on Friday to $230/$240 by the close of the New York COMEX market. Trade talk in New York of a stocks hike and an LME statement saying it was monitoring copper spreads, contributed to an easing of the backwardation, U.S. traders said.
